{{short description|1663 work by Athanasius Kircher}}
{{italic title}}
[[File:Athanasius Kircher (cropped).jpg|thumb|Athanasius Kircher|alt=Athanasius Kircher (cropped).jpg]]

'''''Polygraphia nova et universalis ex combinatoria arte directa''''' is a 1663 work by the [[Jesuit]] scholar [[Athanasius Kircher]]. It was one of Kircher's most highly regarded works<ref name="MuchembledBethencourt2007">{{cite book|last1=Muchembled|first1=Robert|first2=Francisco|last2=Bethencourt|first3=William |last3=Monter|first4=Florike |last4=Egmond|title=Cultural Exchange in Early Modern Europe|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FtidiZurzAgC&pg=PA187|date=March 2007|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-84548-9|pages=187–}}</ref>{{rp|187}} and his only complete work on the subject of [[cryptography]], although he made passing references to the topic elsewhere.<ref name="Lang"/>{{rp|121}} The book was distributed as a private gift to selected European rulers, some of whom also received an ''arca steganographica'', a presentation chest containing wooden tallies used to encrypt and decrypt codes.<ref name="Findlen2004">{{cite book|author=Paula Findlen|title=Athanasius Kircher: The Last Man who Knew Everything|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C0iGO0Hr95UC|year=2004|publisher=Psychology Press|isbn=978-0-415-94015-3}}</ref>{{rp|271}}<ref name="Lang"/>{{rp|120}}

==Background==
Kircher reported that the origin of the work was a request from [[Ferdinand III, Holy Roman Emperor|Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand III]] to develop "a kind of lingua universalis" which would allow written communication between all peoples. The Emperor knew of the earlier secret communication system developed by [[Johannes Trithemius]] in his 1518 work ''[[Polygraphia (book)|Polygraphia]]'', dedicated to the art of [[steganography]],<ref name="Trithemius1608">{{cite book|author=Johannes Trithemius|title=Iohannis Trithemii Steganographia: h.e. ars per occultam scripturam animi sui voluntatem absentibus aperiendi certa|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fQdCAAAAcAAJ&pg=PP1|year=1608|pages=1–}}</ref> and wanted to know if such a system could be used to bridge different languages.<ref name="HAB">{{cite web |title=ATHANASIUS KIRCHER UND HERZOG AUGUST |url=http://www.hab.de/ausstellungen/kircher/vitrine1-4.htm |website=hab.de |publisher=Herzog August Bibliothek Wolfenbüttel |accessdate=28 April 2020}}</ref>

Systems of cryptography had been developed in Italy in late medieval times and by the 17th century many rulers employed cipher secretaries for diplomatic and other sensitive communication.<ref name="Lang">{{cite book |last1=Láng |first1=Benedek |title=Ways of knowledge transfer (chapter) in Real Life Cryptology |date=2018 |publisher=Amsterdam University Press |location=Amsterdam |jstor=j.ctvfp6380.12 }}</ref>{{rp|113}} The [[Thirty Years War]] gave rise to a range of scholarly publications summarising existing knowledge of the field, and there was a growing interest in the relationship between cryptography and linguistics.<ref name="LeeuwBergstra2007">{{cite book|author1=Karl Maria Michael de Leeuw|author2=Jan Bergstra|title=The History of Information Security: A Comprehensive Handbook|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pQBrsonDp6cC&pg=PA297|accessdate=2 May 2020|date=28 August 2007|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-08-055058-9|pages=297–8,321}}</ref> Emperors Ferdinand III and Leopold I, who ruled over empires speaking many different languages, were particularly interested in this field.<ref name="FransenHodson2017">{{cite book|author1=Sietske Fransen|author2=Niall Hodson|author3=Karl A.E. Enenkel|title=Translating Early Modern Science|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J_U4DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA324|accessdate=2 May 2020|date=15 September 2017|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-34926-1|page=325}}</ref><ref name="Findlen2004"/>{{rp|268}}

The Jesuit order played an important role in spreading the idea of mathematics as a kind of universal scientific language. As well as geometry and theoretical mathematics, Jesuit scholars worked on a number of applied projects, including calculating machines such as the one Kircher had designed and then described in his 1637 work ''[[Specula Melitensis Encyclica]]'' and the [[Organum Mathematicum]] he had built for Emperor Ferdinand III. By such means the Jesuits sought to cultivate court patronage and to strengthen and propagate the Catholic faith.<ref name="RB">{{cite web |last1=Batchelor |first1=Robert |title=The Republic of Codes: Cryptographic Theory and Scientific Networks in the Seventeenth Century |url=https://web.stanford.edu/dept/HPS/WritingScience/Cryptography.html |website=web.stanford.edu |publisher=Stanford University |accessdate=28 April 2020}}</ref> Kircher had an established interest in the origins and underlying unity of languages and writing systems, which he explored in various works including ''[[Prodromus Coptus]]'' (1636), ''[[Lingua Aegyptiaca Restituta]]'' (1643) and ''[[Turris Babel]]'' (1679).<ref name="Fletcher2011">{{cite book|author=John Edward Fletcher|title=A Study of the Life and Works of Athanasius Kircher, 'Germanus Incredibilis': With a Selection of His Unpublished Correspondence and an Annotated Translation of His Autobiography.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7Wo-w2sl6zEC&pg=PA40|accessdate=2 May 2020|date=25 August 2011|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-20712-7|page=40}}</ref> He had also studied the [[Voynich manuscript]], although he apparently had no success in decoding it.<ref name="KennedyChurchill2006">{{cite book|author1=Gerry Kennedy|author2=Rob Churchill|title=The Voynich Manuscript: The Mysterious Code That Has Defied Interpretation for Centuries|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF0oDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT82|date=28 August 2006|publisher=Simon and Schuster|isbn=978-1-59477-854-4|pages=82–}}</ref><ref name="JanickTucker2018">{{cite book|author1=Jules Janick|author2=Arthur O. Tucker|title=Unraveling the Voynich Codex|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yzppDwAAQBAJ|date=16 August 2018|publisher=Springer International Publishing|isbn=978-3-319-77294-3}}</ref>

==Introduction==
The title page of ''Polygraphia Nova'' carries an emblem of the hand of the divine creator holding a compass and describing a circle that bears the motto ''Omnia in uno sunt, & in omnibus unum'' ("all things are in one, and the one is in all things").<ref name="Kircher1663">{{cite book|author=Athanasius Kircher|title=A. Kircheri ... Polygraphia nova et universalis ex combinatoria arte detecta, etc|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4_4KFFlnrEgC|year=1663}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Worthey |first1=G. |title=Omnia in uno sunt… |url=https://web.stanford.edu/group/kircher/cgi-bin/site/?attachment_id=797 |website=stanford.edu |publisher=Stanford University |accessdate=26 April 2020}}</ref> This axiom was central to all of Kircher's intellectual work, which explored how phenomena from different countries, different times and different belief-systems all shared fundamental unity. The axiom echoed the earlier beliefs of Catalan [[Neoplatonist]] [[Ramon Llull]] (1232–1316)<ref>{{cite web |last1=Burkart |first1=Lucas |title=Athanasius Kircher und das Theater des Wissens |url=https://www.metaphorik.de/fr/book/export/html/235 |website=metaphorik.de |publisher=Metaphorik.de |accessdate=1 May 2020}}</ref><ref name="Poulouin"/> and the philosophy of [[Bonaventure|Saint Bonaventure]], who believed that divine being permeated all aspects of existence, however apparently different they might be: 'Quia vero est summe unum et omnimodum, ideo est omnia in omnibus' ('But because it is most highly one and in every measure, for that reason it is all in all although all things be many and itself is not but one').<ref>{{cite web |last1=Haase |first1=Fee-Alexandra |title="Parallel Worlds". Clusters for a Theory of Concepts of Communications. Historical Intercultural and Cultural Comparative Studies in Perspectives of National and Transnational Constitutions, Values, Concepts, and Terms of 'Communication' '- 'Orality' - 'Literacy' - 'Rhetoric' - 'Media'. |url=https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/6534/1/MPRA_paper_6534.pdf |website=mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de |publisher=[[Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München]] |accessdate=1 May 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=ITINERARIUM MENTIS IN DEUM |url=http://www.haywardfamily.org/ccel/b/bonavent/journey/journey.htm?fbclid=IwAR2hpcQZHI1JTAFRdzrISkC_nFbaws7jJ6zn_Hjw6lROpXm4UnIdLZBWVoA |website=haywardfamily.com |publisher=Calvin College |accessdate=3 May 2020}}</ref>

In his introduction, Kircher claimed that the book would allow correspondents in any part of the world to exchange letters without speaking each other's languages.<ref name="MuchembledBethencourt2007"/>{{rp|187}} In each section, Kircher acknowledged the work of earlier scholars, and the work thus presented a compendium of approaches not previously brought together.<ref name="DJ"/>

==Section one==
''Polygraphia Nova'' was composed of three sections. The first, ''The Reduction of all Language to One'' offered a kind of translation device involving codes in which vocabulary lists were assigned a two-part symbol - a roman numeral and an Arabic numeral.<ref name="Poulouin">{{cite journal |last1=Poulouin |first1=Claudine |title=Athanase Kircher (1602-1680). Apologétique et crise de l'encyclopédisme |journal=Littératures Classiques |date=2003 |volume=49 |pages=181–199 |doi=10.3406/licla.2003.1956 |url=https://www.persee.fr/docAsPDF/licla_0992-5279_2003_num_49_1_1956.pdf |accessdate=2 May 2020}}</ref>  The first part indicated meaning: Kircher provided 1048 multilingual groups of words arranged over 32 pages in tables organised alphabetically in the order of the Latin column. Thus, for example one entry is "magnitudo, grandezza, grandeur, grandeza, grösse" (greatness). All of these words are assigned the same first-part symbol. The second part denoted grammatical function (e.g. noun ("greatness"), verb ("make great") or adjective ("great")).<ref name="RB"/>

This would allow a writer in one language to record a version of their text in the code so that a reader who did not speak the same language could translate from the intermediate code into their own. It was based on the [[Tironian notes]] system, supposedly devised by [[Cicero]]'s secretary.  In 1624 [[Augustus the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg]] had published a book outlining this system, under the pseudonym 'Gustavus Selenus', and other scholars had also described it.  Kircher's work was therefore not original, but he appended his own universal dictionary, making it a workable system for any rulers who had access to a copy of his book.<ref name="DJ">{{cite web |last1=Jackson |first1=David |title=Early modern universal languages as seen through the thoughts of Kircher |url=http://www.davidjackson.info/voynich/2015/04/12/early-modern-universal-languages-as-seen-through-the-thoughts-of-kircher/ |website=davidjackson.info |publisher=David Jackson |accessdate=28 April 2020}}</ref>

==Section two==
While the first section was concerned with communicating meaning between languages through an intermediary code, the second section, ''The Extension of all Language to All'' allows the conversion of letters into Latin words, regardless of the language encoded.  By this means a word in the original language can be rendered into Latin prose; a reader of the same language can then use the dictionary of Latin words to discover the original letter to which it corresponds. This section was based largely on the work of Johannes Trithemius. Kircher reminded the reader that the purpose of the work was to make possible the conversion of kings and princes around the world, and said that the method he described would allow a message to be written that could be understood in any language.<ref name="Poulouin"/><ref name="Findlen2004"/>{{rp|264}}

==Section three==
The third section, ''A Technologia'' is about the [[Vigenère cipher]]. It explains how to use the tally sticks included in the ''Arca seu cista steganographica'' (steganographic ark or urn), a chest with twenty-four compartments holding 144 sticks that can be used like [[slide rule]]s to rapidly encode and decode messages. Thus Kircher claims, the phrase ''Cave ab eo quem non nosti'' ('beware him who you do not know) can easily be translated into ten languages, including Hebrew, Greek, Arabic and Chinese.<ref name="Poulouin"/>

==Distribution==
Kircher did not keep an organised record of the people to whom he sent a copy of ''Polygraphia Nova'' or the ''arca steganographica'' and their distribution must be inferred from his correspondence.  To further complicate matters, the early exemplars were sent out not with the complete book, but with manuscript versions of one or more of what afterwards became its sections; only later did he follow up by sending the complete book.  Some recipients were sent a book, but not an ''arca''; some were sent directly by Kircher himself, while others were sent through intermediaries to rulers with whom he did not enjoy direct contact.<ref name="Findlen2004"/>{{rp|292}}

The first ''arca'' was sent to [[Ferdinando II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany]] in 1659, and Kircher then sent texts on cryptography to [[Ferdinando II de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany|Emperor Leopold]], [[Archduke Leopold Wilhelm of Austria]], [[:cs:Bernard Ignác Jan z Martinic|Bernard Ignaz von Martinitz]], [[Augustus the Younger, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg]], [[Maximilian Henry of Bavaria|Maximilian Heinrich, Elector of Cologne]] and [[Pope Alexander VII]]. In 1661 Kircher sent an ''arca'' to the Emperor's younger brother, [[Archduke Charles Joseph of Austria]], which turned out to contain a number of errors. The difficulty of using the ''arca'' without a full explanatory manual may have prompted Kircher to produce a single, standard edition of his various manuscripts, and he started sending our copies of ''Polygraphia Nova'' in June 1663.<ref name="Findlen2004"/>{{rp|287–91}}

==Legacy==
Although the work was much admired, as were the chests of tally sticks, there is no evidence that any ruler used them to attempt the translations he suggested.<ref name="Godwin">{{cite book |last1=Godwin |first1=Joscelyn |title=Athanasius Kircher's Theatre of the World |date=2015 |publisher=Inner Traditions |location=Rochester, Vermont |page=18 |isbn=978-1-62055-465-4}}</ref> The only known instance of someone using the techniques described in ''Polygraphia Nova'' is an August 1663 letter to Kircher from his long-time correspondent [[Juan Caramuel y Lobkowitz]], who had also been sent a copy.<ref name="Findlen2004"/>{{rp|283}}

In 1989 [[Eduardo Paolozzi]] created a sculpture fountain entitled ''Polygraphia Nova'' in [[Schwabing]], Munich.<ref>{{cite web |title=Brunnenliste |url=https://www.muenchen.de/rathaus/Stadtverwaltung/baureferat/oeffentlicher-raum/brunnen/brunnenliste.html |website=muenchen.de |publisher=Landeshauptstadt München |accessdate=27 April 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Biography |url=http://paolozzifoundation.org/biography/ |website=paolozzifoundation.org |publisher=The Paolozzi Foundation |accessdate=27 April 2020}}</ref>
